blocks.x: George Justin
My name is George Justin, and I was born in New Orleans on the 17th day of September, 1915.
What part of town were you born in?

That was considered more or less the Tremes section of New Orleans, where there was always quite a bit of activity with the location of the Cooperators Hall, the Economy Hall, and later the San Jacinto Club, which were all wonderful places for jazz, wherein there was always something going on at various times during the week, if it wasn't a dance, as we used to call it a banquet. How do you spell it? That's the term. They used to say banquet, but that's the Creole pronunciation of it, I guess, was banquet.
You know, old Mercinians said they called sorays or something.
Oh yes. Uh-huh. And every time you heard that expression, you always knew just where to go, whether it was the Economy Hall or the Cooperators Hall or the San Jacinto Club.
The Cooperators Hall, is that what they used to call the old Hoax Hall too? It's a church there on Tremes?
It's a church right on Tremes, which was formerly called Liberty Street.
Yeah, I went to church there once.

As a matter of fact, I used to stay right across the street from there, so therefore I had access to the places at various times of the day, and where I'd get a chance to listen to some of the fellas playing and whatnot. And I think it was one of these halls, which when I don't remember, that I got a chance to see some of the guys that were more or less inspiring to me. And one particular fella I had in mind was this Alphonse Piku. However I never had a chance to study under Piku because at that particular time things were pretty rough and conditions were very bad. And the overall conditions just was bad and the only thing about it, the inspiration was there, and from time to time I just got to see and listen to various groups that used to participate over there until I was able to go to school and learn music.
Now where did you go to school? Which school did you go to school?

Well, at that time I went to, I started out at St. Mary's Academy, which was a unit comprised of girls and boys, but later the boys entered the place, was transferred to a little school on St. Bernard Street. Of course I understand that school is there no more, but it was just more or less temporary until they could find a better site.
St. Mary's was down to the cathedral?

That's right, right about, just about a half block from the St. Louis Cathedral. Then from there I went to a Gugman Nicholas School on Gugman Nicholas, and later went to Joseph A. Craig School. And from there I went to Albert Wicker, left Albert Wicker and went to McDonald's 35 and graduated in high school in 1934 I think it was, yes.
Were you a Catholic I suppose?
Yes, I was born and really Catholic. And I left there and went to Xavier University for about a year. And I had hoped to go back, but for some particular reason I just never did get back.
Well can you tell me about the first music you ever heard? Did your folks play, your parents play any instruments?

Well, no, neither of my parents was more or less musically inclined, I wouldn't think so. But we've got a bunch of fellas in the neighborhood have got the experiment from listening to various groups that used to participate in ones at the time. And we used to have what you call bands of our own, wherein one fella played the bass drum which was comprised of an old beat out wash tub. Then another fella would play the kettle drums which was, oh the kettle drum was made out of one of these old antique cheese boxes. I don't know whether you remember seeing those around.
Yeah, I've seen them.

And of course our biggest instrument, wind instrument at the time was what you call a kazoo. I don't know whether you've heard of the kazoo or not, but we had various forms of the kazoo. It was one form, we had it made like a trumpet, and another form it was made like a clarinet. We'd go through the motions and just play a whole lot of the old songs that we used to listen to.
One of our friends, Edward Johnson, they call him Noon, he's not knowing that it has a bazooka.
Oh yeah.
It has a slide. Oh yes, yes, yes.

Well there used to be a group that used to make all these fish fries around that particular time. And one of the fellas I remember very well, he used to call him Sand Paper George. Oh I've heard of him. The thing about it, he used to give the group rhythm, you know, he had pieces of sandpaper, he used to rub them together and you'd be surprised at the type of rhythm you would get from it. And I had noticed him in several places, you know, even sometimes the local spots, you know, in the barrooms, and he'd go in there and he'd join with various groups. And every time there was a band of music on the corner he'd jump on the truck and pull out his sandpaper. So he was particularly musically, he just had that feeling. How old was he? Well he was much older than I was. At that particular time I would say he was around in his 30s, in his middle 30s, of course I was a little bit of a fella myself.
Maybe he's still around in the city. Maybe we can play.

Possibly so. You can never tell. But they had a very unique aggregation wherein he played the sandpaper and another fella played the kazoo and this instrument's built like a bazooka. Of course I don't know where the idea was taken from that instrument, wherein George Burns used to play the bazooka. It could have been.
He probably had those in New Orleans first I think.
Yes. And then too they had another type of instrument which one of the fellas had developed himself. It was made out of a wash tub with a pole running perpendicular from the base of the tub.
Out of the strings.
Wherein it had strings and he could key those strings down and get almost any note you wanted to. And the change was not too far, but in all he got the desired results he wanted to get.
What did you play in that little band?
Well in that little band I used to play the clarinet.
The real clarinet?

No, there was no real clarinet but it was a kazoo made in the shape of a clarinet. Oh I see. And then too I used to alternate from the clarinet to the bass drum, because I used to like to beat the bass drums. And one particular fella around there at that time, I used to call him, I don't remember his name, but you could hear him beat that bass drum miles and miles off and I was more or less inspired there too. And of course this was during the time that when Manuel Perez had his great band. I don't know whether you remember.
I met him once in 1943. Oh you did?
Oh he was a wonderful musician.
Natty Dominic is a pupil. That's right.
Natty studied under Manuel. The only thing I could never understand why he had never gotten the recognition that some of the other fellas had gotten, you know, had contributed so much to jazz.
He quit and lost his teeth, you see, before they ever recorded very much, so he didn't make any records. I guess that's one reason.

Well I heard a different version of it. Of course it could be a lot of truth because they tell me he was the type of man, he never cared too much about socializing and getting out with the boys and drinking and staying out late and all that.
Yeah, so the other fellas would after a job they'd go around that room and he'd take his money and run home. That's right. He was that kind of a man.

And I heard that, so I guess maybe that alone had something to do with it because I have read several books even not too long ago pertaining to various fellas, and they never seem to mention anything too much about him. And I often wondered why they didn't since I thought he had contributed so much and he had developed so many good musicians.
Yeah, they never got the recognition they deserved. No.

But it was a funny thing. When I began to study, I studied under an old professor, and that particular time he was in the post office. And his hobby, he'd always loved music, as a matter of fact he played music himself. And I should think there was more or less a sideline for him.
What was his name?
And his name was, I don't remember his first name, but his last name was Shalini.
Oh yes.

Old Man Shalini they used to call him. He used to be a wonderful trumpet man. And of course he played on the old style along with the old fellas, like Mania Perez and that bunch. What did you study with him? I studied clarinet. I studied clarinet, the old Albert system under him.
How did he teach? Did he make you learn self-edged and ear training and sight singing first, or started you right on the instrument?

Well he started me on the instrument first. First the fingering and how to fingering instrument, basic foundation of the instrument at first. But of course he didn't have too much knowledge I think of ear training at that time, because all the facilities were very poor as far as learning was concerned. You couldn't get the proper methods you want to, or you could study by. And of course I think he had a very wonderful knowledge of music, wherein he taught more than one particular instrument. As a matter of fact he taught clarinet, saxophone, trombone, trumpet, and maybe some form or phases of piano. But of course at that time my brother and myself, we were attending his school at the time.
Well you had a brother who played.
Yes. He was playing, he started out playing alto saxophone and I started out playing clarinet.
We both started at the same time. Older?
Well he's, I should think he's about a year and a half or two years older than I am.
Is he still in New Orleans?
He's still in New Orleans but he's not active in music anymore.
Do you have his address? If you could tell him maybe we can interview him.
Well offhand I don't know his address, I'll have to look for it. Of course I could give you my mother's house and you could always contact him from there.
Well yes, if you might put it on here.
Well okay, well if you'd contact Mrs. Alice Justin at 1429 Domaine Street. Oh yes. It's right across the street from the old San Jacinto Club.
I recorded there. I recorded George Lewis and Buck Johnson. Oh did you? Yes, in 1944. I recorded there one whole week, six nights. Oh, that used to be quite a spot.
Well do you remember the old Lions Club which is located about three blocks from there? No. Near Claiborne Street.
I remember that.
Oh yes, that was quite a spot too.
There's a carnival club, a white carnival club uptown they call Lions Club uptown.

No, this was a club, it was on the same basis as San Jacinto's Club. And I think the club I always thought was in competition with San Jacinto's Club. And they used to always try to outdo one another by having various bands and of course at that time they used to call them Buck Dancers and of course we'd call them Sessions now and see which had the best group and whatnot. But as of now it's been converted to a funeral parlor now. Oh I think I know. So that's why you probably haven't paid any attention to it and I think it was converted way back, as far back as 1933. Well I know. 33 or 34. I have a picture of a funeral, a brass band, right in front of it and I know where it is.
Yeah, well of course at that time my grandfather was president of the club.

As a matter of fact he himself turned into a funeral parlor. And because he had his place out there on St. Philip Street between Murray and Liberty. What's his name? Raul J. Lopes. He was the Lopes of the coin, the Lopes establishment on St. Philip Street.
Yeah I remember another funeral parlor on St. Philip too.

That's right. But under Professor Chalini I enjoyed my music very much. As a matter of fact I didn't get as much out of it as I should have or I could have because at that particular time, being the youngster you know you always come home from school, throw your books on the couch or the machine and you go out and play some ball, football or baseball or basketball or something of that particular nature, until I was reminded of the fact that I had to go to lessons. And the very good thing about it, lessons was I would say very expensive. I thought they were very reasonable.
But did it charge?

Twenty-five cents a lesson. Twenty-five cents a lesson, which I thought was very reasonable. Of course at that time money was scarce and for that particular time of the year and in New Orleans you didn't take, you didn't need too much money to operate or as you might say, or you didn't need too much money to live. And we got to learn our instruments pretty well while we was invited to play with the post office band. The post office had organized a band and he was the director at the time. So I was particularly fascinated by this venture because of the fact I would be out in the streets just like the rest of the fellas was playing. Sort of a brass band? Yes, that's what it was. Uh-huh. And usually on anniversary days and memorial days we'd get out to the post office and play and it was particularly exciting.
You played B flat clarinet I guess?
Yes, the old Albert's sister.
Did you ever play E flat?

No. Well the only time I played E flat was in service. I played in service for about four years during the last war from 1942 to 1946. And but speaking about this old post office band, I was particularly interested in it and really enjoyed it for the simple reason that we used to rehearse twice a week. And we used to rehearse at different fellas' homes, you know.
Did most of the fellas work at the post office?

Well I'd say about half of them, or maybe a little more than half, worked at the post office. Well I think that was a general idea to comprise a band with members of the post office. And well I got a big bang out of it for the simple reason. We'd rehearse twice a week and we'd have such a good time after the rehearsals. And that's the thing I always looked forward to was the food and drinks afterwards, you know. And it was the same condition. I guess I could have been a heck of a lot more advanced than I was if it wasn't for the good times that were centered around that particular time. I could remember another incident where I was working with a cousin of mine at the time. He was a saxophone player. His name was Dejean. Did you know Dejean? Harold Dejean? Yes. I've seen him in the, he played a parade a couple of weeks ago. Al Crocise has his own band now. Oh is that right? I haven't seen him.

I haven't seen him in about three or four years since, of course I've been away from New Orleans for quite some time now since. When did you leave about? Well I left in 1936. I left there on the Steema Capitol. I was playing with Sidney Desveen at the time. And we played the boat for that summer. Went all the way up the river.
And he played a parade a couple of weeks ago.
Al Crocise has his own band now. Well, he has his own band now.
Oh is that right? I haven't seen him. I haven't seen him in about three or four years since, of course I've been away from New Orleans for quite some time now since. When did you leave about?
Well I left in 1936.

I left there on the Steema Capitol. I was playing with Sidney Desveen at the time. And we played the boat for that summer. Went all the way up the river. All the way to St. Paul, yes. So I left the unit in St. Paul because I got pretty sick. And I started going back to New Orleans where I just came here to Chicago since my closest relatives was here. And I've been here ever since. Of course I have been tempted to go back several times during that period but I never did get back.
Tell me a little more about Manuel Perez when you heard his band. Where was it? Economy Hall?

Well I used to hear Manuel's band most of the times. He seemed to have been the favorite band leader for these funeral parades and whatnot. Well how long? Because that used to be customary every time some member of some society had passed and they used to always have a funeral band.
They still have them.
But they're not as frequent as they used to be.
Well there'd be maybe two a week almost.
Even now?
Even now in the uh…
Is that right?
We don't hear about all of them but there was one a week ago today. Uh-huh. Kit Howard, I don't know if you remember. Yeah I used to work with Kit Howard.
He had one last Sunday afternoon. I worked with Kit Howard. I wasn't there. I left town.
A friend wrote me this week and said he found me.
Is that right?

There were three parades last Sunday. One across the river and then two over on the side. Is that right? And then in addition to that there was Kit Howard at the funeral. Is that right? Well anyhow I used to remember Manuel Perez because he was always so powerful.
You could hear him by three or four blocks. And everything he played was so clear and concise I mean you could hear everything he blew.
Do you remember the name of his band?
Well I think at that time they used to call his band the Excelsas.
Uh huh.

I think that's what it was because they used to have about seven or eight piece units. And I think he used to play for various engagements I think when the old roof garden was in prominence a long time ago. And that's one of the first places I ever- Gravier? That's right. Right there on Gravier. The Pitian Temple.
That's right.
The old Pitian Temple. Still there.
They call it the Civic Center building. They tore all that part down. Yes I heard about it. The City Hall was right there across there.
Well that was one of the first spots I did get a chance to listen to when I was able to get out by myself.
And Manuel Perez played up there.

Yeah. Sometimes I even went out there with relatives. To have a social affair I'd get up there and of course most of my time was spent on the bandstand. I never cared too much about dancing but I just loved to listen to the music and try to find out to see what was going on. And of course at that time, at that particular time they had several fellas that I used to think were some of the greatest musicians I had ever heard in my life of course.
I'm sure they were. Yeah.

But of course I would consider myself at that time not too much of a good judge of music or talent because I didn't know too much about it. But I could remember fellas like Buddy Petit and Sam Organ, old Sam Organ, and Chris Kelly, Kid Renee, and matter of fact I worked with Kid Renee for a while when they first opened up the New Gypsy Tea Room in 1932. Oh yeah, there on St. Philip and St. Philip.
In 1932. When they first opened up there I worked with him.

He and his brother and another fellow from the old school by the name of George Augustan. He used to play banjo at the time. As a matter of fact I think his father used to be a musician. Augustan? His father was there.
I heard that old man a lot.

Uh-huh. And out of the whole group I used to like Kid Renee very much, very much because he had very good ideas, he had a beautiful tone, and he was an inspiration to a whole lot of fellas because I remember some of the fellas used to come up there and just sit up there and watch him and listen to him and even make comments. I'd say, boy I suddenly wish I could play like that guy. But he was a happy-go-lucky fella and he didn't seem to worry about anything. He just loved to play his music and loved to have his little drink every now and then, which was more or less customary at the time. And I find that musicians in that particular area they got a lot of enjoyment out of playing and having a good time. Now whether any money was made out of the deal I don't particularly know or I don't remember. But yet still they seemed to be happy at all times. They'd never done anything but playing music. I don't think I can remember any of the fellas from the old school doing anything but playing music.
Just brought a few of them then. Yeah. Was Kid Renee your favorite trumpet would you say?
Well he was one of my favorites, yes.
He's one of my favorites. How about Buddy Petit? I never got to hear him at all.

Buddy Petit was very good too. I didn't hear him too very much, not as much as I had listened to Kid Renee or even Chris Kelly because Chris Kelly used to stay out of my neighborhood there. So I used to get a chance to listen to that in practice all the time. But I understand that I think Buddy Petit, he used to work at a little place on St. Bernard Street, he used to call it Alley. And he had worked there and of course that was out of my jurisdiction and I wasn't allowed to go that far. But the only experience I had gotten was from various times where I would listen to him on the truck advertising for a dance that night or a dance that Monday night or maybe listen to him in the street parade or something like that. But in all there was a whole lot of inspiration there, very much.
Do you remember much about Chris Kelly?

Yes I remember a whole lot about Chris Kelly because he used to be the favorite blues trumpet player. I used to like to hear him play the blues more than anybody else. And I just imagine I could see him now playing the blues with perspiration just rolling off his forehead and everything like that.
It was a very picture. I've never even seen a picture of him. How big a fellow was he or what did he look like?
Well let's see, he wasn't too big of a fellow, I don't imagine.
He was as tall as you?
Well I said he would have been taller than I am and a little heavier. I figured maybe about a hundred and seventy, seventy-five pounds like that.
Fairly, fairly big then.
Yes, fairly, not too terribly big. Because I can't remember too much about him because this was a very long time ago and I
was a pretty little fellow, you know? Do you remember did he use mutes or anything or what style of trumpet did he play?

Well he played somewhat of a growl style. They used to use the derbies during them days. Of course the derby hat was very popular. And they'd use the derby and the sink plunger, the plungers that some of the guys use today. They used to use that type of plunger. But very seldom the other mutes style, the cup mutes style. Well it was more or less the plunger and the derby.
Where did you hear Chris Kelly? What sort of places? Was it the halls or?

Well this is at the Economy Hall, I think. I heard him there and I heard him several times on one of these advertisement trucks. I heard him there and I heard him there and he was at one of these famous, what you might call banquets, you used to call a long time ago, Bonquet, which was I think was the Creole pronunciation of it. Yeah. Do you know Creole by the way?
Do you talk that?
No, I don't talk Creole, not as much as I would like to. Of course my mother and father both speak very well.
Did they learn the regular French too?

Yes, they learned French, I guess it was handed down to them from their mothers and fathers. But I guess maybe one of the reasons why I didn't learn too much about it, because I was probably out in the streets someplace trying to see what's going on. And the only thing about it, I noticed when they used to have company and they were talking about something that they didn't want kids to know anything about, so they immediately went into Creole. So we were completely lost and we'd have to leave. So we were getting nothing out of the conversation anyhow. So I find it very fascinating and the thing that I liked about Rene, he used to do a number in Creole just about every night. And he used to bring the house down.
Do you remember what it was?
Well, the name, the number was He La Ba.
Well, Rene did that.
Yeah, he used to do that, He La Ba.
I still sing it.
I noticed that Paul Barberin has got a recording on that in the stereophonic tape, which is very modern now. I would like to hear it. I've never heard it, but I've seen it advertised.
I haven't heard that particular tape. Yeah. Albert Burbank sings it. Well, Piku does too now. Oh yeah, yeah.

Well, those were the guys that used to sing it, like Piku and Kid Rene and some other fellas. Quite a few of them used to sing it because it was very popular. And a lot of times it was popular during the Mardi Gras too. Yeah, it was supposed to be a Mardi Gras.
Yeah. Were there any other Creole songs similar to that that they used, Rene or any of the others?
No, I don't think so. I don't remember too much about any other than that. But I remember it so much because at the time I was working with Rene, he used to do it just about once a night.
And he could sing it for a long time because he made words himself.

He made all the words himself. And of course from time to time there was always somebody in the audience that knew what he was talking about, knew what he was saying. And they in turn inspired the other people that didn't know what was going on to sort of get with the program as you might say.
That's a nice, joyful number.
Yes, very much so. But I left New Orleans on the steamer capital in 1936 I think it was, yes.
Sidney Desveen was leader?

Yes, he was leader of the band, that, ever since band then. And I worked with fellows like, well, Judge Raleigh, I don't know whether you know him or not, but incidentally he's in Chicago too. Judge Raleigh, he is a drummer.

That's right. Charlie Elgar gave me his name a long time ago when we were, Natty Dominic was playing some dances. Oh, is that right? And we needed a drummer because Baby Dodds wasn't so well, wasn't able to play the whole dance, so we had two drummers.
Yeah, well I wish I had known him. I could have gotten contact for you. Jasper Taylor, but Raleigh is from New Orleans. Judge Raleigh.
Yeah. Judge Raleigh.

Next time I'm here I'll try to get to talk to him. I never met him. He used to be a fine drummer too. Is he fairly young or old or something? Well, I think he's about my age. He might be a year or two older than I am, but not very much more than that. Then there's another fellow in Chicago too from New Orleans, his name is Ransom Nolan. But he wasn't, I don't think he was born in New Orleans, but he had moved to New Orleans at an early age and he stayed around there. And he worked with several of the bands around New Orleans. Of course I could remember some very fine units that had come from the old style groups, come from fellas that had taught younger fellas like the fellas that worked with A.J. Peerron. I don't know whether you remember A.J.

Peerron. No, I met his widow. I knew Clarence Williams, his partner in the music business. Yes. I went down there to meet him one year and he died a few months before and I talked to his widow that summer.
Well, there was another group that had a very good band at that particular time and it was called the Sonny South Syncopators.
Well, who was in that? You never heard about that?

I don't think so. Well a cousin of mine was playing for his first trumpet, Leo Dejon, Harold Dejon's brother. He's got a brother out there in the west coast now. And there was another fellow by the name of Joe Phillips, he played trumpet. He plays in the bass. Yeah, incidentally he was one of Chalini's pupils, one of Chalini's dark pupils. And there was another fellow by the name of Sidney Montague, he played drums.
I've heard of him, I don't know him.
Eddie Pearson, I know you know Eddie Pearson.
Oh yeah, sure. Yeah, trombone. That's right.

He was one of the main stems in the group. Eddie Pearson and let's see, there was another guy who played a wonderful clarinet. His name was Elliot. What was Elliot's last name? Well I don't think he's in New Orleans now. I think he left New Orleans a good while ago.

Who were some of the other clarinetists you heard when you were a small boy? You mentioned Piku. Can you think of any others? Do you remember Big Eye Louis for instance? Louis DeLille was his real name.
Louis DeLille? Yes. I remember him very well. Big Eye Louis.
How did you hear him?

Yeah, I used to hear him in those walking parades. And I used to hear this George Lewis too when he won the parade, too. Because I think at that time he was playing E-flat clarinet. I don't know whether he's playing E-flat, no, no.
He fell out, as he says, in the parade about four years ago. Oh, is that? The sun got him out, almost like a sunstroke. He hasn't played hardly a parade since.
Yeah, I remember him. And then too there's another fellow by the name of Humphrey. Yeah, Willie.
Willie Humphrey? Yeah, he still plays Paul Barber.
Yeah, well I think he come up later.
His father played too, back in the old Eagle Band 1910 to 1915 up there.
And there was somebody else down there, a very wonderful clarinet player.
You don't, no, you wouldn't remember George Bocquet?

No, I remember Peter, Peter Bocquet. Peter Bocquet. Peter Bocquet, I think he, I remember him, because I think at the time I left New Orleans he was President of the Union. But no, I don't remember Peter, the other fellow that played clarinet. But I remember an old trombone man back there, used to call him Jim Robinson I think, big,
tall, slender fellow. Yeah, yeah. He plays George Lewis. Oh yeah.

dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear
Wait a minute. This is . There it's going now. Is he ever going to tell about Pirone? Oh, yes.

I was going to say about Pirone. I had seen some particular fellow, a lady in years there was this big image of Pirone. I always thought that the two could pass for brothers. Now, if you remember Ben Burnie, if you saw Ben Burnie, you saw A.J. Pirone because it looked so much alike. And I think they both had short legs, right?
I didn't know that Burnie, I knew that I heard that about Pirone.

Yeah. Well, I think Ben Burnie, his leg was something he used to wear one of these raised shoes or something like that. Now, whether it was the same leg or not, I don't know. But I always thought any time you saw A.J. Pirone, you saw Ben Burnie. And of course Pirone, he used to have a very wonderful band and most of his dates were the society dates you might consider. He played for the lights or what you might call the four hundreds.
Yeah, and he played down at the Spanish fort I guess.
Right.
Did you ever go out there, was that sort of an amusement park? Spanish fort?

Yeah. Yeah, it was. They used to give picnics out there all through the day wearing it. You'd play out there all day and they'd fish and they'd swim and they'd come in and they'd have drinks and serve food and they'd go out and fish again. It was out from the water, you know. Is that out on the lake? Out on the lake, yes.
Because the fire of St. John comes through there.
That's right.

There's nothing there at all. Is that right? They filled in the lake, you know, it goes out another half a mile. They filled that in and built houses. People live out there. Is that right? No amusement. What about West End? Do you remember anything about that when you were a boy?
Not too much about West End, no.
There's the West End blues, you know, that Oliver and Louis and Oliver made. Yeah.
I used to hear it played around there but I never knew too much about it.
Was Millenburg going when you were a boy?

Millenburg, yes. That's where they used to go out on the beach down, Millenburg, and I think that's where the song more or less was derived from, this Millenburg joy. Yeah. And it was a funny thing. I didn't know, as much as I had played with Paul Barber, and I just found out not too long ago that he had written this number, the Bourbon Street Parade. I didn't know that. You didn't remember that? No, it did not until I went down to Jazz Limited one night. I talked to Freddie Coleman and another buddy of mine was down there, I worked with him in New Orleans, his name was Warden Joseph, trombone man, and they called him Frog. Yeah. Well we happened to be talking and they asked him, I said, what's the name of this last number you played? They said, well that's the Bourbon Street Parade. I said, Bourbon Street Parade. So I said, whose number is that? He said, Paul's number. And I was so surprised I didn't know what to do because they didn't know. Well to begin with, when he organized, he wasn't playing them kind of tunes. Because he had written some tunes I think when he was in New York with Lois Russell's band.
When I came back, Sweet Papa. Yeah. A couple of others.
And well I remember one particular one that we used to use as a theme song, which was called I think, To Your Picture in the Frame.
Oh yeah.

I don't know what I've heard of. Yeah. Your picture in the frame. Well I remember that very well because of the fact that we used to open up all the dance engagements with it. And I used to close, so therefore I remembered it very much. And when he came down there he got some of the fellas from the band I had been working with at the time. And this band was comprised of fellas that used to go to school together, you know, and we called ourselves and at Crescent City I had us. And we more or less took care of all the school engagements and what have you, and various parties and picnics we used to play. And we had one fella from the old school work with us for quite some time. And as a matter of fact he was in charge of ours. We made him in charge of this group since we thought he knew so much about it. And his name was Bigfoot Bill. I don't know whether you had the occasion to meet him or not, but he was a drummer. And he had played around New Orleans with several bands a long time ago. Now whether he was born in Ridd there or not I don't know, but I can remember he joined our group and he helped us quite a bit. And we had a piano player by the name of Wiggins, he was very nice.
Yeah he still plays at a place called Lutyens.
Well I'll tell you there were several fellas in the world.
With Toca, do you remember Lawrence Toca? Well that's not his real name, there's another name he has, a trumpet player. Lawrence Toca. He was very short, small, so. Lawrence Toca.
How did it came up later? He was not young.
Well I'll tell you there were some of them, two other fellas that more or less inspired

me and had worked from time to time as a teacher of mine, and whom I liked very much, and liked the styles very much. I don't know whether you've had the occasion to meet a fellow by the name of Albert Gishard. No. But he played with the Robichaud unit. They had a terrific unit there. That was during the time when they used to work at a place on Rampart Street called the Paradise Inn.
That's the Joe Robichaud.
Joe Robichaud, yeah. George Lewis now. Oh is he playing again?
Oh yeah, sure.
And he played with Lizzie Miles for several years.
He was on television with Lizzie in February. Is that right? I thought he had some other means. No. No. Because when I saw him several years ago on a visit home. He'd be here next week.

With who? With George Lewis out at the Hunt Club, out way real far west. The Hunt Club? Yeah, on 12th Street, about 5,000 or so something west. 5,000 west. Yeah. Yeah. On Hunts Street. On Hunts Street. How long are they going to be out there? How long are they going to be out there? How long are they going to be out there? With who?
With George Lewis out at the Hunt Club, out at Wave, real far west.
The Hunt Club?
Yeah on 12th Street, about 5,000 or so something west.
5,000 west? Yeah. On Hunt Street?
On 12th Street.
Well how long are they going to be out there?
Just about four days I think, or a week.
Yeah well I'll have to get out there. Might be some guys playing with the group I still know.
George Robichaux was with George for the last year now. He came up to me if you want to have some money.
You cut that out.
Let's see who are we talking about? Some of the old Robichaux's bands.
Oh yeah.
Have you played with Robichaux?

No, my brother played with Robichaux. He played with him for a long time. Well you see at the time he was playing with Robichaux, oh I think I had left Desvene because I played with Desvene a year, not quite a year. And I came to Chicago and stayed in Chicago. But all during that time he was playing with Robichaux at the time. He and Sam Dutre and Dennis Gishard and Cyril August and.
Sam Dutre, that's the younger Sam Dutre I guess. His father was an old time.
Yeah, his father was an old time. Did you ever hear him? No, I've never heard his father.
Well Manuel Mineta talks a lot about Manuel Mineta studied clarinet with Sam Dutre. We'd been on the boat years ago. Oh yeah. When Louie first started out in 18, 18 or so. Uh huh.
He was on the boat.
Is that right? Sam Dutre taught him to use the double embouchure. How did you learn? Did you cover your upper teeth too?
No.
You bite onto it.
Yeah. That's the same way that Mr. Charlin taught me.
He taught you that way.

That's right. He said never put your lip over your top teeth because you would always have a tendency to cut it. And I had noticed that some of the fellas had used that particular system even later in years. And how they managed to blow like that I do not know.
It was supposed to be a French system. And Manuel Mineta says if you bite onto your teeth you're going to wear your teeth down, which some of them do. That's right.
If you know of some of the musicians who play with an instrument, there's an arch in their
teeth.
Yeah. And just like some of the fellas that blows a trumpet or trombone you know so they have the corn on that. Yeah. But I had-
Bobby Bigard uses that double embouchure and some of the French players do too.
Uh huh. Well one thing he got good results out of it because he was a pretty powerful man for a long time.
Do you remember any of the other clarinetists, how they held their instrument, if anybody else did that, that you ever from New Orleans had?

No, I don't remember anybody else that was more or less playing in an unorthodox style. Most of them? Most of them followed the same pattern. Yeah. And the only thing that I have found with the clarinet players in New Orleans is that they never seem to get away from the old Albert system. You find three-fourths of them a day still playing the Albert system. Yeah, Simeon and I.
Sidney Bechet, same way.

Yeah. Johnny Donnells. Bonnie Bigard, Johnny Donnells, the same thing. And yet still the BAM system is supposed to be the, well, which is a developed system, and you have several ways of making a passage of notes, more so than you had with the.

It's a little easier for trills and a lot of fast work you can do better on it. I guess it's better in tune. Yes, that's right. But did you ever think, did you ever try the BAM? Did you play the BAM much?
Yes, I played the BAM in the Army at the time.
Did you still use Albert though?
No.
Well you used the BAM.
Yes, I had used the BAM quite a bit. After some of the fellas had told me about it and I had the occasion to use it, I find it very helpful. Yeah, it's easier.
You didn't have to stretch as far either.
That's right. But what about the tone?
Do you think there's any difference? Does the Albert have a bigger tone or more? Well I don't think so.

I don't think, I don't look at, I think the tone qualities come from the person himself. And it was a good sound instrument and you've got a pretty good tone, but I think the tone is developed more or less by yourself.
Yeah, probably.

I think so. And some instruments, I would say this, it has a flatter tone and some has a sharper tone. I mean you could detect a difference if you play a type of instrument and you are satisfied with the type of tone that you get. Of course most musicians with a good tone is never satisfied. They are always striving to get the ultimate, which we never seem to regain. But yet and still we know what we want, but we can't seem to get it, but yet and still it's pleasing to somebody else. You see what I mean? It's pleasing to somebody else, but yet and still we strive for that perfection, we strive for that perfection, but we never seem to get what we want. But yet I notice in some instruments the tone qualities are sharp in one particular instrument and sometimes it's flat in another particular instrument. Of course my instrument I had, it was a long time before I could detect anything because to begin with I had a crack in the horn I didn't even know I had. You see? And it got an instrument at such a very cheap price I was just too glad to get it. But it wasn't.
I'm not trying to pry into your personal affairs. How much did you pay about when you first got it?
I paid about, I think my father paid about eight or nine dollars for it.
Yeah, some kind of thing is an opportunity for that.

I didn't know that in the case. Even today you could. Yeah, and it was through this particular friend of mine, this fellow by the name of Alfred Gishaw, he told me that the instrument wasn't no burden. I thought it was all right, you know, and they had about two cracks in it, one at the top and one at the bottom. Did it leak pretty bad?
Did it get hard to blow?

Well it was very hard to blow, very hard. And being in the Albert system too and just learning how to play and trying to make one particular note which would be natural was supposed to be the hardest note to make on it because you had to stretch so, you know. And I found it very difficult at first, but I later got adjusted to it. But it wasn't until later until I found out what the real reason was.
So had you ever played a little kin fife or anything like some of the kids do to learn your fingering first?
No. The only—
It was just kazoo. Did you finger the kazoo any or just sing it?
Well they had three holes in it, but there wasn't too much control with it. The only tonal control I would say would be from the top if you held your hand on the top and raised it up from—

Well I think I would like to interrupt what you're talking about. But on the parades when you were a kid, do you remember if any of the kids would go along beside the second line as they call it, and play any little instruments or fife or anything
like that? Oh no, no, no. They were just so glad to get along with the music and march with the music. The very few times I noticed anybody trying to play along with the group.
Yeah I have heard some times that they might have done at a certain period play some of
those kids.
Possibly so.

You don't remember ever singing? No. I should think that everybody was so glad that they could be a part of the group. You know, wherein some of the kids would get out there and they would dance on the corner and they would run up ahead of the band and wait until the band meets them and after they meet them they run a block farther.
They still do.

You see? But I don't know, for some particular reason I don't think the setting is what it used to be and it's not like it used to be. People don't feel the same way they used to and I don't know, I find it very different. And I was surprised to find out that there are so very few musicians working out on Bourbon Street. You know, the type of music that they love so well.
Not in the neighborhoods either.

There used to be no, every little corner of the band. No, there's nobody in the neighborhood. Not now. The Cooperators Hall is gone, the San Jacincense is gone, the Lions is gone, the Bowles is gone, the Bowles Club is gone, the Frons Amis is gone. Well of course I guess they used that Frons Amis from time to time.
It's a church now I think.
Oh is it?
Pretty sure it's a church. And so is the economy. The old Perseverance Hall up in there too is a church.
That's right. Then there was this place on St. Bernard Street right near Carpus Christi. I don't know if you've.

Well there's a place called New Hall along in there. Yeah. A little bit off of that on Durban Street, the Artesian Hall, it's still going. Most halls may still, New Hall might have music sometimes, but not much at Artesian Hall.
Well I was trying to think of this place on St. Bernard Street. There used to have.
Oh wait, there's another big Autocrat club.
Autocrat club, that's what I'm thinking about, the Autocrat. They still have it?
They still have it?
They've been there. They used to have some very nice affairs there. But all in all, I don't know, what's really going on?
Well the jukeboxes have knocked out a lot of this. Yeah that's what I guess so. The saloon bands and that.

But it's a funny thing, I used to remember people a long time ago when he said these fish fries, on Saturday, any time you saw a red lantern out there on somebody's front door you know it was going to be a French.
That's what it was. That's right.
It hanged on the red lantern. You saw that red lantern on the front and people used to scrub the steps a long time ago and get it wiped. Where'd they set the lantern?
Hang it on.

Well they'd hang it from the gate. You know those gates there that hang it from the frame of the gate where it would protrude the gate. Yeah. Just enough that you could see it in any direction you were walking. And the nicest thing about it, I thought about it, was it was so cheap. You could get a fish sandwich for a nickel or a fish sandwich for a dime or two slices of bread, a potato salad.
Did they charge admission to get into the place?

No, there was no admission. But you could always find music going on right there. There was always a piano and any time you found a piano there was always a piano player. And that's how I used to remember this Burnell San Diego so terribly well. Oh yeah, that's right.
I was a little out of hand because I never got to there.

Because he was, matter of fact we stayed right next door to each other. You know he lived on one side of the house and I lived on the other side of the house. And there was always somebody playing on that piano from the day from morning until night. And there used to be quite a confusion about getting on the piano because he, his brother and his sister, all of them played.
Was that up on Liberty Street about?

That's right. That was on Liberty Street because at that time I was staying on Liberty Street right across from the- Oh. From the- The Walk Raiders Hall. 925 North Liberty Street. Nice. Of course that number was 929, right next door. And there was always confusion about getting on the piano. You know who our kids are. They want to beat the brother to the piano. And of course Burnell I used to think he had exceptionally good talent. And I used to hear some of the fellas talk about him, what a wonderful left hand he had. And it was during the year 1936 I think when Earl Hines came down to New Orleans. It was 1936 or 1936 or 1935 around that time. And anyhow, Earl Hines had made an appearance in New Orleans there. He played at Pelican Roof Garden that night. And during intermission Burnell was up there on the bandstand playing the piano and he got a chance to listen to Burnell so he said, he made a remark, he said, well I'd never heard a fella like this play before. I had never heard a fella with such a tremendous left hand.
Really sensational. Really sensational.

And as a matter of fact you could always find good piano players with right hand. But whenever they had a good left hand they had Sonny. And he was that type of musician. He was well liked by everybody and I don't care wherever there was a party and he was always around. And I don't care who was playing piano, they had to get up and let Burnell play.
Now what type of musician was it? Did he read music? No he didn't read music. He was more or less gifted.
He was a musician? No.
He was more or less gifted.

But he could play almost anything? Almost any style you wanted, whether it was jazz, Dixie, or swinging, he could imitate almost any piano player you could possibly name. And at that particular time I think, this time when Hines was down there, Hines was pretty popular. And I know from time to time he used to play like Earl Hines, you couldn't tell the difference. And he was just the type of fellow, he was just completely at home with the piano, he was relaxed and everything. And any place he went, I mean they'd have a piano he'd have to sit and play. And I don't care who was playing the piano, they'd have to get up and let Burnell play. He loved his piano and it was too bad. I mean he couldn't be here today because I, oh yes he died awfully young, very young. And he could have been, he was a lot of inspiration to a whole lot of fellas because there was always fellas that wanted to play like him. He played in some of the bands too?
Or mostly by himself?

Not particularly, mostly by himself. But he played with a small group there, some group of singers that he used to work with from time to time. But he, you could never depend on him. No, that's one thing about him, you could never depend on him. But he looked like he would much rather, you know, just go from here, go from this place to that place, and you know, just play a few and take part in the party and whatnot. Because everybody liked him so well, and he was a likable fellow too.
Can you tell me a little bit more about the fish fries? Was that similar to a lawn party? Did they have them outdoors or in the house?

No, well, depending on how the weather was. But most of the fish fries that I had been to was more or less the inside. Inside? Yeah. You'd go over there and you'd buy fish and you could eat it there, you could even take it out. And of course that was during the prohibition days too, you could always buy a little home brew too. You know, and so I guess that's why some of the fellas used to come around there too, they'd get their little home brew and they'd drink their little wine and they'd have a boil until four or five o'clock in the morning. And the aroma was always so inviting, that's the thing I found so fascinating about it, to see the red larynx sitting on the outside and the red front. They used to pound the red brick a long time ago and they'd scrub the sidewalk with this red brick and when it dries off it made it nice and pretty. Well red color. Red color. Red color. Because you know a long time ago all the sidewalks were made with nothing but brick. It wasn't here until recently in the last few years that they started paving the streets, but most of the sidewalks was comprised of nothing but brick. And by the time, as a matter of fact when we were nothing but kids we used to sell red brick. Five and ten cents a bucket. That used to be. Powered it up. Powered it up.
That used to be our sideline.
Well we'd go to various lots, you know. Old houses had been torn down and we'd mass them in the wagon and roll them on the arm and pound it up. How'd you pound them up?
I'm going to try breaking one of them up.
Well with some kind of hard object or hammer or something like that. Yeah, anything.
It doesn't get gummy or anything. No.
Well it gets a little gummy because if you notice the red brick, it rains down there all the time. It was always raining. And the brick themselves, it stayed constantly damp.
Very damp, yes.

That's what it was. So therefore it had a pretty good body to it. Yeah. It was cold and it stayed more or less together but very few times you would get it. It would be in such a powdered form that it would blow away. Yeah. You know. And even the humidity down there would help to keep it damp. Yeah. And they found out that it was a very good solution. They used to mix up grammer powder with this red brick and used to scrub the steps. What kind of powder?
Grammer powder.
It's a type of powder similar to the washing powders you have today. Oh yeah. But I remember that particular name because it was a popular brand there.
Yeah, like soap powder.

That's right, and my mother used to save the coupons from it. Oh yeah. But they used to have coupons with it, you know, along with the octagon soap and all that. And they used to have a mixture wherein they'd mix it up together and scrub the steps and naturally get through and then wash the sidewalks with the brick. And by the time the steps was dry and the red brick was dry it was just like this red rug sitting on the floor. Of course it wouldn't last very long depending on the time of the year it was and how much rain you would have. But naturally it would give it a very good setting and the aroma from the fish would give it a very good setting and more or less appetizing. And if you see it, you pass by it, you say, oh, this smells good, well we'll stop by and see. And then when you get inside, I mean there was so much going on that you would be glad to stay if you had any money in your pocket. You were going to stay for a while. And then the fellas would come by there from time to time and they would play. And one thing I had found in New Orleans, there was a whole lot of people that could always play the piano if they couldn't do anything else. They were more or less musically inclined people. And I wouldn't say that too much of them had training as far as learning music, but they were more or less gifted and they had the incentive to play, you know. That was natural music. Natural music and they played what they felt and not what they heard somebody else. You know they had their own ideas about it. And I have often wondered why a lot of people didn't spend too much time trying to cultivate the ideas, you know. But as I said before they were more or less happy-go-lucky people and they were just satisfied enough to have some place to stay and no food to eat and they were particularly satisfied. And the monies that they were getting, I wouldn't say that they were getting fabulous prices because I remember when I played my first date I worked for six hours for a dollar and a quarter. And when I got my best job I think I went with Sidney Dancefein and played a gig in Mobile, Alabama. Played one night in Mobile and we made seven dollars I think that night and I thought I was the richest person in the world. Well it just goes to show you, you know. Of course I was in school at the time. But lots of times even if we didn't get anything we were satisfied just to know that we could play and we enjoyed playing and I've always worked with a bunch of fellas that enjoyed playing. And it's like I went to see a buddy of mine and I felt terribly sorry about him. I don't know whether you had the occasion to meet him or not but he had played around New Orleans for quite some time. As a matter of fact we worked together in Sidney Dancefein's band and his name was, we used to call him Wiggles. Did you know Alton who plays piano?
Yeah, Alton Pernell.

Alton Pernell. Well this boy's name, his brother, Thereto Pernell. Yeah he was one of my teachers also. He taught me quite a bit because he had played much longer than I had and I used to go to his house for lessons. But he had a stroke about two years ago, I said two or three of them since that time.
Yeah.

And every time I'd go down there I used to go by and see him. But he was one fellow he really learned fast. I mean he's a good musician, he could read anything, he could put in front of him, he could play anything. And on top of that he had such a beautiful tone, beautiful tone. And I would say that he played a different style from anybody else because he didn't play Dixie or he didn't play progressive but his style was more or less on the gut bucket style. And that's what they used to feature a long time ago.
You mentioned records with Lee Collins.

Right. And if you was the type of musician you couldn't play a gut bucket style, you were just lost. And there was another guy down there who was a tremendous musician. I also found out that he wasn't much of a reader either and this was this, what was his name, Handy? Oh John Handy.
Did you run across the fellow named Handy? Oh yes, he still plays, yeah. Oh is he?
Yeah. He was another fellow that Heinz had commented on because there was a time.
He's about the best alto sax around there now. No I don't know. He plays clarinet too.
Oh he plays clarinet too. I can't think. Well did you meet Son Johnson in New Orleans? I can't think.
Son Johnson. Son Johnson.
No.
Very wonderful clarinet.
Very, he played alto saxophone and he played clarinet too. I can't think. Well he played, let's see, he was playing with the Moonlight Serenaders.
No, no, no.

You ever run into the fellas with the Moonlight Serenaders down there? No. No. What was this fella, big tall, like fella, he was a guitar player. He was in charge. I think at one time he was president of the local down there.
Houston was?
Not Houston, before Houston's time.
I don't know who that was. Now Louis Cottrell is president.
Well Cottrell is recent. Because Cottrell used to play with Don Albert, right? Yeah. But Sidney Cate. Oh yeah. Remember Sidney Cate?
I met him, yes.

Yeah, well Sidney Cate used to be in charge of the union at one particular time. He's secretary now. Yeah. Well he had a band, they called themselves the Moonlight Serenaders. And during the time when I was playing with this young group I had mentioned about earlier the program about the group that was comprised of fellows from school. Well anyhow, Son Johnson was playing with him. And I remember quite a bit about Son because of the fact that he also played with this WPA band that was organized in 19, just after Prohibition. Yeah, they used to play in the park there, at the playground, every Wednesday or Thursday. And we used to make special efforts, you know, to get down there and listen to the music. We'd play a while. Which park was that? It was Lemon Playground, right on Basin Street. You know where Basin Street? Yeah. Right there. Well it's called Lafitte Street. Oh yeah, sure I know. It's Lafitte Street. That's right. And it was just after this new playground had been inaugurated, this Lemon Playground, and then they'd start having his bands come out there. And well if you looked at the fellow you would never think he could play a note. You know he looked so unconcerned about everything and dressed casual and he had several opportunities to go with various bands out east and he never went and I understand that he had gone someplace for a while and he got tired after about a week and a half and came back home. I mean the same thing goes true for a fellow like even Pernell, Theodore Pernell. He's had several opportunities. But I know for some particular reason the fellows never wanted to leave home.
Well we're about out of tape here. Is there any other thing you'd like to add about your own life or anything else before we quit?
Well the only thing about my, I just was sorry that I just stopped playing, period. Because I don't think there's anything else that I would rather do than play.
Well maybe there's still a chance.

But the thing about it, when I came out of the Army I was pretty sharp I'd say this because I had played with the service band for four years. But I also came out with the wife. So therefore I had to sort of look out for myself and the wife and the way the country was in such a condition. And the trend had deviated from the big bands to the small combinations and it just appeared to be a dogfight for recognition because the field had gotten so crowded. And musicians were just plentiful around Chicago, plentiful. And so I decided maybe I'd better go on back to the job that I had because I knew that I could make an honest living and a fairly decent living. And I said well maybe I would practice from time to time just to sort of keep up my instrument. And then I had joined the Army Reserve Force and I was a part of that for about two years. About four years but we didn't seem to get too much out of it because then they started reverting everything to military personnel and just taking some away from the music end of it you know. So therefore they-
Well I hope you do get back to it sometime again because-

Yes. I'd like to get back because I don't think there's anything I would much rather do than play music. Because I enjoyed every bit of it. Very much so even though I didn't make much money but I had a whole lot of fun. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
